### Tidy time series packages

This workshop is about **tidy** time series in R.

Install them with:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
# The tidy forecasting packages
install.packages("fpp3")

# Time classes, time graphics, and features
install.packages(c("mixtime", "ggtime", "feasts"))
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/david-pisnoy-46juD4zY1XA-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Tidy time series packages

```r
# Data manipulation
library(dplyr)
# Plotting functions
library(ggplot2)
# Time series class
library(tsibble)
# Tidy time series datasets
library(tsibbledata)
# Feature extraction and statistics
library(feasts)
# Grammar of time series graphics
library(ggtime)
# Semantic time vectors
library(mixtime)
```
::: {.fragment .fade-in}

![](resources/fpp3.svg){style="height:200px;float:right;padding-left:10px;margin-top:-50px"}

### Time series data

Comes in all shapes and sizes!

Like all data, we hope it's tidy :broom:

::: {.callout-tip .fragment}
## All time series data contain...

* The time of the observation (*index*)
* One or more observations (*measurements*)

:::{.fragment .fade-in}
Some datasets have identifying metadata,

* Identifying variables for the series (*key*)

### The tsibble data format

![](resources/tsibble.png){.sticker-float-right}

A tsibble is a tibble for time series!

The quarterly visitors to Australia are found in the `tourism` dataset.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
library(fpp3)
tourism
```

::: columns

```{r}
#| message: false
library(fpp3)
as_tibble(tourism)
```

:::{.callout-tip}
## Column types

In this dataset, the column types are:

* `index` variable: [`Quarter`]{.fragment .fade-in}
* `key` variable(s): [`Region`, `State`, and `Purpose`]{.fragment .fade-in}
* measured variable(s): [`Trips`]{.fragment .fade-in}

## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Representing time indices

![](resources/mixtime.svg){.sticker-float-right}

Time is surprisingly tricky to represent!

* frequency
* granularity
* time zones
* calendars
* leap years (and seconds?!)
* holidays
* civil/absolute time
* time periods

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/jon-tyson-FlHdnPO6dlw-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Representing time indices

![](resources/mixtime.svg){.sticker-float-right}

```{r}
tribble(
  ~`Granularity`, ~Function,
  "Annual", "`year()`",
  "Quarterly", "`yearquarter()`",
  "Monthly", "`yearmonth()`",
  "Weekly", "`yearweek()`",
  "Daily", "`date()`",
  "Sub-daily", "`mixtime()`"
) |>
  knitr::kable(booktabs = TRUE)
```

:::{.callout-tip}
## Sub-daily granularity

`mixtime()` finds the granularity (e.g. 30 minutes), `datetime()` uses seconds.
:::


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/jon-tyson-FlHdnPO6dlw-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Time arithmetic

![](resources/mixtime.svg){.sticker-float-right}

Numbers shift time by its granularity:

```{r}
#| echo: true
yearmonth("2026 Nov") + 0:2
```

Durations shift by calendar units:

```{r}
#| echo: true
date("2026-01-31") + months(1L)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Differences are durations too:

```{r}
#| echo: true
date("2026-12-25") - date("2026-11-30")
```
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/jon-tyson-FlHdnPO6dlw-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Linear and cyclical time

Linear time moves forward, cyclical time repeats.

```{r}
#| echo: true
today <- date("2026-11-30")
yearmonth(today)
month_of_year(today)
day_of_week(today)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Cyclical time is useful for finding specific seasons.

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Is it a weekday? (Saturday is day 6)
day_of_week(today) < day_of_week(6L)
```
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/jon-tyson-FlHdnPO6dlw-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Mixing granularities

Time of different granularities can be combined...

```{r}
#| echo: true
c(
  year(2026L), yearmonth("2026 Nov"),
  date("2026-11-30")
)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
... but only converted when the result is certain.

```{r}
#| echo: true
year(yearmonth("2026 Nov"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| error: true
# Weeks can span two months!
yearmonth(yearweek(date("2026-11-30")))
```
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/jon-tyson-FlHdnPO6dlw-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Using mixtime with tsibble

mixtime vectors can be the index of a tsibble.

Let's update the datasets used in this workshop.

```{r}
#| echo: true
tourism <- tourism |>
  mutate(Quarter = yearquarter(Quarter))
aus_production <- aus_production |>
  mutate(Quarter = yearquarter(Quarter))
PBS <- PBS |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(Month))
aus_retail <- aus_retail |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(Month))
vic_elec <- vic_elec |>
  mutate(Time = mixtime(Time))
pedestrian <- pedestrian |>
  mutate(Date_Time = mixtime(Date_Time))
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
interval(vic_elec)
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/jon-tyson-FlHdnPO6dlw-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}

Tidy time series data uses tidyverse tools!

::: {.callout-caution}

## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Manipulating time series data

However there are some differences when working with time...

The time `index` is always preserved (implicit `group_by()`).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Grouping across time

Sometimes you want to summarise over time.

Summarising over all of time is no longer a time series, so first convert to a tibble with `as_tibble()`.

To re-index by a new variable, use `index_by()`.
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/randy-fath-R5_1N6ZgCOo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Temporal aggregation

```{r}
#| echo: true
aus_gas_annual <- aus_production |>
  index_by(Year = year(Quarter)) |>
  summarise(Gas = mean(Gas))
print(aus_gas_annual, n = 4)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-important}
## Complete years only?

`time_is_complete_at(Quarter, cal_gregorian$year)` finds which observations are in years with all four quarters.
:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/randy-fath-R5_1N6ZgCOo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Visualising time series

Time series visualisation helps us identify *time series patterns*.

These patterns include:

* trends
* seasonalities
* cycles
* covariates
* events

They also help identify anomalies/outliers.

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/nathan-dumlao-5Hl5reICevY-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Time plots

The most common time series graphic is the "time plot", created with `autoplot()`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
pbs_scripts <- PBS |>
  summarise(Scripts = sum(Scripts))
pbs_scripts |>
  autoplot(Scripts)
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/nathan-dumlao-5Hl5reICevY-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}

## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Time plots of mixed granularities

`stat_summary_time()` aggregates in the plot.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 3.5
aus_production |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Quarter, y = Gas)) +
  geom_time_line(colour = "grey60") +
  stat_summary_time(
    granule = years(1L), fun = mean,
    colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1
  )
```

Incomplete years (2010) become `NA`.

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/nathan-dumlao-5Hl5reICevY-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}

## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Lag plots

A lag plot compares observations with those before them, coloured by season.

```{r}
#| echo: true
aus_production |>
  gg_lag(Gas, geom = "point", period = years(1L))
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/nathan-dumlao-5Hl5reICevY-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}


## {}

### From lag plots to the ACF

::::: {.morph-slide}

```{r}
#| label: beer-acf
#| cache: false
#| output: asis
beer <- aus_production |>
  filter(Quarter >= yearquarter("1992 Q1")) |>
  select(Quarter, Beer)
acf_morph(
  beer, Beer, id = "beer-acf", pause_lag = 4,
  alt = "Animation of a time plot of quarterly beer production becoming lag plots, and the autocorrelation of each lag plot becoming a bar of an ACF plot."
)
```

:::: {.morph-captions}

::: {.morph-step}
Quarterly Australian beer production since 1992.
:::

::: {.morph-step .fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Shift a copy (blue) by one quarter, pairing each observation with the one before it.
:::

::: {.morph-step .fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Each pair is a point in the lag plot. The first observation has no pair.
:::

::: {.morph-step .fragment .fade-in-then-out}
The autocorrelation $r_1$ is the linear relationship in this lag plot (blue line).

It is small and negative: the first bar.
:::

::: {.morph-step .fragment .fade-in-then-out}
At lag 2, quarters are paired with those half a year earlier.

Peaks meet troughs, so $r_2$ is strongly negative.
:::

::: {.morph-step .fragment .fade-in-then-out}
At lag 3, quarters are paired with the next quarter of the previous year.

Like lag 1, these are neighbouring quarters.
:::

::: {.morph-step .fragment .fade-in-then-out}
At lag 4, quarters are paired with the same quarter a year earlier.

Peaks meet peaks, so $r_4$ is large and positive.
:::

::: {.morph-step .fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Continue for lags 5, 6, ...

The seasonal lags 8, 12 and 16 are strongly positive too.
:::

::: {.morph-step .fragment .fade-in-then-out}
The ACF plot: one bar for each lag plot.

Bars beyond the dashed lines are unlikely for uncorrelated data.
:::

::::

:::::


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### ACF plots

An ACF plot shows autocorrelations (lagged relationships). This helps to identify trends, seasons and cycles. Lags are durations (e.g. 12 months).

```{r}
#| echo: true
pbs_scripts |>
  ACF(Scripts) |> 
  autoplot()
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/nathan-dumlao-5Hl5reICevY-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}

## {}

### Which is which?

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: acf-match-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| warning: false
library(patchwork)
cowtemp <- read.csv("resources/cowtemp.csv") |>
  as_tsibble(index = time)
mink <- read.csv("resources/mink.csv") |>
  mutate(time = year(as.integer(time))) |>
  as_tsibble(index = time)
us_deaths <- as_tsibble(USAccDeaths) |> mutate(index = yearmonth(index))
air <- as_tsibble(AirPassengers) |> mutate(index = yearmonth(index))
series_plot <- function(x, title) {
  autoplot(x, value) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = title)
}
acf_plot <- function(x, title) {
  autoplot(ACF(x, value)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = title) + ylim(-0.5, 1)
}
year_axis <- scale_x_mixtime(time_breaks = years(4L), time_labels = "{lin(year)}")
(series_plot(cowtemp, "1. Cow temperature (daily)") | acf_plot(us_deaths, "A")) /
  (series_plot(us_deaths, "2. Accidental deaths (monthly)") + year_axis | acf_plot(cowtemp, "B")) /
  (series_plot(air, "3. Air passengers (monthly)") + year_axis | acf_plot(mink, "C")) /
  (series_plot(mink, "4. Mink trappings (annual)") | acf_plot(air, "D"))
```

- [x] 1B, 2A, 3D, 4C
- [ ] 1B, 2D, 3A, 4C

## {}

### Seasonal or Cyclical?

These common patterns are commonly confused, can you tell them apart?

::: {.callout-tip}
## What's the difference?


Seasonal patterns have...

* **Consistent** and predictable shape,
* Repeats with a **fixed time period**

Cyclical patterns have...

* **Inconsistent** shape and amplitude,
* Repeats with a **variable time period**

:::

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Time series decomposition

Decomposition separates time series patterns into individual series.

::: callout-tip

## Additive decomposition via STL

$$y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t$$

* $y_t=$ data at time $t$
* $T_t=$ trend-cycle component at time $t$
* $S_t=$ seasonal component at time $t$
* $R_t=$ remainder component at time $t$

:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/laura-geror-lGeAZjIhQyo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Additive & multiplicative patterns

STL only works with additive patterns

$$y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t$$


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
library(ggplot2)

i <- 1:119
pattern_types_demo <- tsibble(
  time = yearmonth("2000 Jan") + i,
  season = sin(i*2*pi/12),
  trend = i,
  remainder = rnorm(length(i)),
  index = time
)
pattern_types_demo |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(season, trend, remainder)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = value, group = name)) +
  geom_time_line() +
  facet_grid(vars(name), scales = "free_y") + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/laura-geror-lGeAZjIhQyo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Additive & multiplicative patterns

$$y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t$$

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
pattern_types_demo |>
  autoplot(trend + 10*season + 3*remainder)
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/laura-geror-lGeAZjIhQyo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Additive & multiplicative patterns

$$y_t = S_t \times T_t \times R_t$$

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
pattern_types_demo |>
  autoplot((2 + season) * trend * (5 + remainder))
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/laura-geror-lGeAZjIhQyo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

### Additive or multiplicative?

::: columns

  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |>

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Additive or multiplicative?

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |> 
  autoplot(Turnover)
```

::: fragment

::: callout-important
## Multiplicative!

STL won't accurately decompose the patterns in this data.

:::

:::


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/laura-geror-lGeAZjIhQyo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### STL for multiplicative patterns

While STL doesn't work directly with multiplicative patterns, we have a *transformational* trick :magic_wand:

::: {.fragment .fade-in}

\begin{align}
y_t &= S_t \times T_t \times R_t\\
\log(y_t) &= \log\left(S_t \times T_t \times R_t\right)\log\\
&= \log(S_t) + \log(T_t) + \log(R_t)
\end{align}

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Other transformations

Multiplicative patterns aren't always *exactly* multiplicative. Instead we often use power transformations via `box_cox(y, lambda)`.

More info: <https://otexts.com/fpp3/transformations.html>
::: 
:::


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/laura-geror-lGeAZjIhQyo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### STL decomposition

Estimate with `STL()`, then access the components with `components()`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4|5"
library(feasts)
dcmp <- tourism |> 
  summarise(Trips = sum(Trips)) |> 
  model(STL(Trips)) |> 
  components()
dcmp
```

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### STL decomposition

STL decomposition effectively separates trend and seasonality from the data.

This helps to more clearly see the underlying changes over time.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Fine-tuning decomposition

While the defaults usually work well, it's worth learning how to adjust the decomposition for better results.

More info: <https://otexts.com/fpp3/stl.html>
::: 


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/laura-geror-lGeAZjIhQyo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

### Fine-tuning decomposition

```{r}
#| label: stl-windows
#| cache: false
turnover <- aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |>
  mutate(Turnover = log(Turnover))
webr_slider(
  turnover, x = "Month",
  fn = function(data, t_window, s_window) {
    fit <- stl(ts(data$Turnover, frequency = 12),
      s.window = s_window, t.window = t_window
    )$time.series
    data.frame(
      `log(Turnover)` = data$Turnover, trend = fit[, "trend"],
      season_year = fit[, "seasonal"], remainder = fit[, "remainder"],
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  },
  sliders = list(
    t_window = list(
      label = "Trend window", value = 21, min = 7, max = 441, step = 2,
      log = TRUE, ticks = c(7, 13, 21, 51, 101, 441)
    ),
    s_window = list(
      label = "Seasonal window", value = 13, min = 3, max = 55, step = 2,
      log = TRUE, ticks = c(3, 5, 7, 9, 13, 19, 27, 55)
    )
  ),
  subtitle = "STL(log(Turnover) ~ trend(window = {t_window}) + season(window = {s_window}))",
  height = 460
)
```

When is the trend too wiggly? When is the seasonality too rigid?


## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Seasonal adjustment

Seasonally adjusted data removes seasonal patterns to clearly see underlying trends.

Adjusted data is in the `season_adjust` column.

```{r}
as_tsibble(dcmp) |> 
  autoplot(Trips, colour = "#aeaeae") + 
  geom_time_line(aes(y = trend), colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_time_line(aes(y = season_adjust), colour = "hotpink")
```

Most datasets contain many related time series identified by one or more keys.

For example, `tourism` contains 304 series.

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Time series features

Instead we can calculate **features** of the time series, which summarise patterns over time.

```{r}
#| echo: true
tourism |> 
  features(Trips, feat_stl)
```

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Time series features

STL decomposition based features include:

::: callout-note
## Seasonal strength (`season_strength_year`)

The signal to noise ratio of seasonality from 0-1.

$$\max\left(0, 1-\frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(S_t+R_t)}\right)$$
:::

::: callout-note
## Trend strength (`trend_strength`)

The signal to noise ratio of trend from 0-1.

$$\max\left(0, 1-\frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(T_t+R_t)}\right)$$
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/jon-tyson-FlHdnPO6dlw-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}


## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Plotting features

These features can then be plotted to reveal the patterns and structure of many series.

```{r}
#| label: features-plot
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 5.5
tourism |>
  features(Trips, feat_stl) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = trend_strength, y = seasonal_strength_year, col = Purpose)) +
  geom_point() + facet_wrap(vars(State))
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/jon-tyson-FlHdnPO6dlw-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}

### Time components [(extra)]{.smaller}

![](resources/mixtime.svg){.sticker-float-right}

Split time into linear and cyclical parts.

```{r}
#| echo: true
time_components(
  date("2026-11-30"),
  year = lin(year), month = cyc(month, year),
  day = cyc(day, cal_isoweek$week)
)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Use the same parts to parse text.

```{r}
#| echo: true
time_parse(
  "30/11/2026", format = paste0(
    "{cyc(day, month)}/{cyc(month, year)}/",
    "{lin(year)}"
  )
)
```

## Unsplash credits

::: {.callout-unsplash}

## Thanks to these Unsplash contributors for their photos

```{r unsplash}
#| echo: FALSE
#| cache: TRUE
library(httr)
library(purrr)
unsplash_pattern <- "([A-Za-z0-9_-]{11})-unsplash\\.jpg"
slides <- readLines("index.qmd")
matches <- regmatches(slides, regexpr("backgrounds/[^)]+unsplash\\.jpg", slides))
images <- unique(basename(matches))
ids <- unique(sub(paste0(".*", unsplash_pattern), "\\1", images))

get_unsplash_credit <- function(id) {
  fallback <- sprintf("* [Photo](https://unsplash.com/photos/%s)", id)
  my_response <- tryCatch(
    httr::GET(
      "https://api.unsplash.com/",
      path = c("photos", id),
      query = list(client_id = Sys.getenv("UNSPLASH_ACCESS"))
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(my_response) || httr::http_error(my_response)) return(fallback)

  xml <- content(my_response)
  name <- xml$user$name
  if (is.null(name)) return(fallback)
  desc <- xml$description%||%"Photo"
  width <- max(0, 60 - nchar(name))
  sprintf(
    "* %s: [%s%s](%s)",
    name,
    strtrim(desc, width),
    if(nchar(desc) > width) "..." else "",
    modify_url("https://unsplash.com/", path = file.path("photos", xml$id))
  )
}
htmltools::includeMarkdown(paste0(map_chr(ids, get_unsplash_credit), collapse = "\n"))
```
